title: Connecting with Connectors
hook: An index card with one useful introduction beats a plea for access to the busiest person.
counterintuition: The paradox is that connectors notice you faster when you stop treating them as the prize. Their scarce attention opens when your first move strengthens the network they already serve.
tryThisNow: Choose one connector and write the useful person, pattern, or resource you can bring before making any request for their time.
keyTakeaway: Approach connectors through contribution. Show that you understand the network they serve and can add value before you ask for attention.

breakdown.fastRead:
The index card in Colin's hand lists the civic data meetup organizers by name. One organizer knows everyone in the city's open-data circle, and Colin wants her attention. His first draft asks for a meeting. His better draft offers a volunteer who can clean transit-stop data for the group's next map night.

Connectors are not shortcuts. They are people with scarce attention and many relational obligations. A useful approach gives them something relevant to pass along, improve, or place.
breakdown.deepRead:
A connector's value comes from the network around them. They hear many requests because other people can sense that access flows through them. That makes a needy approach weak from the start. It adds one more demand to a person already sorting demands.

Contribution changes the posture because the connector sees you serving the circle, not just seeking lift.

Connor sees this on an angel investor office-hours clipboard. Ten founders have written their names for five-minute slots, and every one wants advice or funding. Connor can wait his turn and pitch. Or he can lead with a pattern from three founders in the room who all need the same regulatory attorney, then offer to introduce the attorney he worked with last year. The investor now sees someone improving the room, not merely asking to be lifted by it.

Paul Revere works as a connector marker because the role is bigger than status. Some names stand for the fact that information and opportunity move through people who are trusted by many circles. Treat that person as a trophy, and you miss the function. Serve the network they care about, and your approach makes more sense.

A connector is listening for fit between your offer and the network they protect.

The mistake is to chase the connector as if proximity itself were the prize. You ask for a meeting because they are famous locally. You ask for an introduction because they know everyone. You ask to be remembered before giving them any reason to remember you. A better move starts with relevance: here is a person you should meet, a pattern your network is facing, or a resource that would help the people who already trust you.
breakdown.fullRead:
Dylan holds a teacher training cohort roster while the program director answers questions from three sides of the room. The director connects new teachers, principals, curriculum specialists, and funders. Dylan wants her attention for a literacy project, but the obvious ask would sound like every other request for access.

He studies the roster instead. Four trainees are placed in rural schools that will need bilingual family-night materials by September. Dylan has already built a parent handout that can be adapted in two languages. His first message does not ask the director to champion his project. It says he noticed the rural placements, can share the handout, and would be glad to adapt it if useful for those trainees.

That is how you approach a connector without becoming another drain. You show that you understand who is around them and what those people need. The attention you ask for is tied to contribution, not entitlement.

What would make the connector look generous, accurate, and useful if they passed your name along?

Eric learns the same rule at a restaurant supplier tasting panel. A tasting spoon rests beside three sauces while the distributor at the table moves between chefs, growers, and store buyers. Eric wants shelf access for a small producer. Instead of pitching the producer first, he mentions that two chefs in the room are asking for lower-salt pantry staples and offers to introduce the producer because the sauce was built for that exact constraint. The distributor is being given a useful match, not a favor request wearing a nicer shirt.

The limit is important. Contribution is not manipulation with better manners. Do not invent value just to get near someone. Do not offer an introduction that helps you more than it helps the people involved. Connectors remember who makes their network stronger and who creates cleanup work.

Niklas sees the difference at a philanthropy roundtable. The placards show foundation officers, nonprofit directors, and city staff. A prominent convener sits two seats away, and Niklas wants a private conversation. He predicts the direct ask will show confidence. Then he hears two nonprofit directors describe the same data-reporting burden. Niklas can connect them with a university analyst who has already built a reporting template. The convener notices because the network got lighter.

Amina misses this at an indie game developer showcase. A controller sits on the demo table, and she spends the evening trying to meet the one publisher everyone is chasing. Later, she realizes the stronger move was available all along: three solo developers needed localization testers, and she knew a community group looking for portfolio projects. When she made that connection the next day, the publisher's assistant replied because the message helped the showcase ecosystem, not just Amina.

Connectors respond to people who make the network easier to serve. Bring them relevance. Bring them good matches. Bring them information that helps the people they already carry. Access follows contribution more cleanly than pursuit.

planSpec.stakes: access, trust, or momentum can be lost if civic data meetup organizer list becomes another generic networking move

examples.scenario: The index card bends in Colin's palm as he reads the civic data organizer list. He must decide: ask the best-connected organizer for time, or offer the volunteer who can clean transit-stop data for her next map night. The transit data is useful today, which makes his later request feel earned instead of imported. The organizer can use the cleaned data without holding a separate meeting first.
examples.whatToDo: Lead with the volunteer and the map-night need. Ask whether that help fits before requesting any separate meeting.
examples.whyItMatters: Colin approaches through contribution. The organizer can see value for the group before giving him attention.

examples.whyItMatters: The connector receives a useful pattern, not another demand. Connor earns attention by improving the network around the investor.

questions.prompt: A civic data organizer knows everyone in the local open-data circle, and a newcomer wants her attention before the next map night. What is the strongest first approach?
choices: Ask for a meeting because she is the most connected person in the room.
Offer a volunteer who can clean transit-stop data for the group's next map night.
Ask her to introduce him to every organizer after the event.
questions.explanation: The volunteer offer helps the organizer's network before asking for attention. The other choices treat her connections as access to extract.

questions.prompt: At investor office hours, a founder notices three other founders in the same queue need the same regulatory attorney he knows from last year. What should he lead with?
choices: His pitch, because his five minutes should focus only on his company.
A request for the investor's personal phone number.
The shared pattern and an offer to introduce the regulatory attorney.
questions.explanation: The attorney introduction shows Connor can improve the network around the investor. A self-only pitch or personal-access request ignores the connector role.

questions.prompt: A teacher-training director connects rural trainees, principals, and funders, and four rural placements will need bilingual family-night materials. Which message best approaches her as a connector?
choices: I noticed four rural placements may need bilingual family-night materials; I can adapt a handout if useful.
I would like you to champion my literacy project with everyone you know.
Can you tell me which principals are easiest to persuade?
questions.explanation: The handout offer serves people in the director's network. The other options ask for influence before offering anything useful.

questions.prompt: At a supplier tasting, two chefs ask for lower-salt pantry staples while a distributor nearby moves between chefs, growers, and buyers. What should the supplier advocate do?
choices: Pitch the producer's full story to the distributor immediately.
Frame the producer as a match for the lower-salt need and offer a useful introduction.
Ask the distributor for shelf access before anyone else reaches him.
questions.explanation: The lower-salt match gives the distributor a useful connection to make. A full pitch or rushed shelf ask centers the advocate's needs.

questions.prompt: A philanthropy convener is surrounded by nonprofits struggling with reporting burdens, and a participant knows an analyst with a tested template. What is the connector-smart move?
choices: Ask the convener for a private meeting before anyone else does.
Offer the analyst and template to the nonprofits facing the reporting burden.
Wait until after the event to mention that he noticed the problem.
questions.explanation: The template helps the network the convener serves. Private access and delayed observation do less to prove useful relevance.

questions.prompt: A developer spends a showcase chasing the one publisher everyone wants, while several peers need localization testers she can provide through a community group. What is the strategic failure?
choices: She treats the connector as a prize and misses a chance to strengthen the surrounding network.
She should have chased more publishers to increase the odds.
She should avoid helping peers because it may distract from her own demo.
questions.explanation: The missed tester match shows status pursuit crowding out contribution. More chasing or less peer help would repeat the same weakness.

questions.prompt: Someone says connectors are shortcuts: get close to one and you get access to everyone in their circle. Why is this weak as a relationship move?
choices: It ignores the connector's responsibility to protect and serve the network.
It works only when the connector is famous enough.
It should be paired with a louder pitch.
questions.explanation: Connectors are not access machines. They are trusted because they judge fit and protect relationships, so contribution matters first.

questions.prompt: A connector receives two messages. One asks for access. The other names a recurring problem in the connector's network and offers a credible resource. What should stand out?
choices: The access request, because directness saves time.
The resource message, because it shows relevance to the network before asking for attention.
Neither, because connectors only respond to people they already know well.
questions.explanation: The resource message shows network awareness and contribution. Direct access without value adds work, and prior familiarity is not the only path.

questions.prompt: Two people approach a high-leverage organizer. One praises her status. The other brings a relevant introduction for two people she serves. Which is stronger?
choices: The praise, because connectors need to know they are respected.
They are equal if both messages are polite.
The introduction, because it strengthens the network the connector cares about.
questions.explanation: The relevant introduction proves respect through usefulness. Praise may be pleasant, but it does not reduce the connector's workload or help the network.

reviewCards.front: How should you approach a connector?
reviewCards.back: Approach with value for the connector's network before asking for attention, access, or an introduction.

reviewCards.front: Why is status-chasing weak with connectors?
reviewCards.back: It treats the connector as a trophy or shortcut. Connectors respond better to people who understand and strengthen the network around them.

reviewCards.front: What kind of value can you bring a connector?
reviewCards.back: A relevant person, useful pattern, credible resource, timely introduction, or clear problem the network already faces.

reviewCards.front: What question should you ask before contacting a connector?
reviewCards.back: Ask what would help the connector serve their network more accurately, generously, or efficiently.

reviewCards.front: How do connectors remember you well?
reviewCards.back: They remember when you make their network stronger and create less cleanup work than the average request.

implementationPlan.title: Bring Value To The Network
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice approaching high-leverage people by serving the network around them before asking for scarce attention.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you contact an organizer, then offer a resource or person that helps the group they already serve.
If you approach an investor, then name a useful pattern or introduction in their ecosystem before pitching.
If a connector supports many participants, then offer something that helps those participants directly.
If everyone is chasing one connector, then first make a useful match among the people nearby.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one connector you want to approach. Write down one person, pattern, or resource that would help their network before you draft any ask.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a high-leverage contact and ask whether your last message strengthened their network or merely requested access.
